exercise:
1. Find your own failure case. Recall a time you asked an AI assistant something about your own systems, codebase, or documentation and got a confident wrong answer. Classify it: was it stale, private, or a provenance failure? Most real cases are two of the three at once, name which.

2. Write the two clocks from memory. Close this page. On paper, list the stages of indexing time and query time in order. Check yourself against the table above. You will use this skeleton every single day of this course, so it's worth getting into memory on day one rather than day ten.

3. Make one prediction. In the note box below, answer in one line: what do you think will turn out to be the hardest part of building a good RAG system? On Day 100 you'll read this back. Getting it wrong is more interesting than getting it right.
html:
Every language model ships as a fixed set of weights. Whatever it absorbed during training is frozen into those numbers, this is its parametric knowledge. It is fast (no lookup, the knowledge is the computation), fluent, and completely static. That last property is the whole problem.

Three things parametric knowledge cannot do

These are not edge cases. They are the reason the entire field exists, and you will recognise all three from your own work:

  • It goes stale. The weights were fixed on a certain date. Anything that changed after, a deprecated API, a new schema, last quarter's numbers, is either absent or, worse, confidently wrong at the old value.
  • It never saw your data. Your internal wiki, your incident reports, your firmware release notes, the PDF someone emailed this morning. None of it was in the training corpus, and none of it ever will be.
  • It cannot show its work. Ask a model why it said something and it will generate a plausible-sounding justification, because that is what it does. There is no pointer back to a source document, because there was no source document. For anything auditable, this alone disqualifies it.

Why fine-tuning is the wrong tool

The instinct is to train the model on your documents. Resist it, and understand precisely why, this is one of the most common expensive mistakes in applied AI.

Fine-tuning is excellent at teaching a model behaviour and form: a house writing style, a domain's vocabulary, a structured output shape, a classification boundary. It is poor at teaching facts you will need to update:

  • Every update means another training run. Your documents change daily; your weights cannot.
  • You still get no citations. A fine-tuned model blends your facts into the same opaque soup as everything else.
  • You cannot reliably delete a fact. When a document is retracted or a customer invokes their right to be forgotten, "retrain and hope" is not a compliance story.
  • New facts can degrade old capabilities, the model drifts in ways your evals may not catch.

The insight behind RAG is to stop trying to change the model at all. Change the input instead.

The reframe: closed book to open book

A model answering from its weights is a student taking a closed-book exam from memory. Retrieval-Augmented Generation hands that same student the textbook, already open to the right pages, and says: answer using only what's in front of you.

Two things follow immediately, and both matter more than they first appear. The model no longer needs to have memorised your domain, it needs to be good at reading. And the answer becomes traceable, because you know exactly which pages you handed over.

The shift is from "how do I get the knowledge into the model?" to "how do I get the right text in front of the model, at the moment it is needed?" That second question is an information retrieval problem, and information retrieval is a mature field with fifty years of theory behind it. That is the good news, and most of what you will learn here.

The two clocks

This is the structural idea to take away today. A RAG system runs on two separate clocks, and almost every engineering decision you will face is really a question of which clock the work belongs on.

Indexing timeQuery time
RunsOffline, once per document (plus updates)Online, once per question
Stagesparse → clean → chunk → embed → storeembed query → search → rerank → assemble prompt → generate
BudgetMinutes to hours. Amortised over every future question.Milliseconds to seconds. Paid again on every single question.
Cost shapeOne-time per reindex, proportional to corpus sizeRecurring, proportional to queries × context size

Notice the asymmetry in that last row, because it drives real architecture. Expensive work at indexing time is often free in practice, you pay once and every future query benefits. Expensive work at query time is paid forever. This is why a technique like contextual retrieval (Day 44) can afford to call an LLM once per chunk at indexing time, while adding one extra second to every query would be unacceptable.

What "augmented" actually means

Strip away the vocabulary and the augmentation step is string concatenation. The prompt that reaches the model looks like this:

Answer the question using only the context below.
If the context does not contain the answer, say so.

<context>
[chunk 1 text]
[chunk 2 text]
[chunk 3 text]
</context>

Question: [the user's question]

That's it. There is no special channel, no weight update, no memory. The retrieved text enters the model through exactly the same door as the question, as tokens in the context window. Hold onto this: it explains why a poisoned document is a genuine security problem (Day 76), why context length is a budget line (Day 79), and why the model can be told to refuse (Day 65).

The claim this entire course orbits

If the right chunk is not in the retrieved set, no model, however large or capable, can produce a grounded answer. Generation cannot recover information that retrieval discarded.

Stated as an inequality: your end-to-end groundedness is bounded above by your retrieval recall. If the correct passage appears in your top-k for only 70% of questions, then 70% is your ceiling, and swapping in a better generator moves nothing. You would be tuning the wrong half of the system.

This is why Days 56–70 are given entirely to measurement, and why the first real metric you will learn is recall@k. It is also why practitioners repeat, almost as a mantra: most RAG failures are retrieval failures. You will spend a lot of this course learning exactly how retrieval fails, and how to tell.

Where the next 99 days go

Days 2–14 build the pipeline by hand, from TF-IDF vectors to a working end-to-end system, so nothing downstream is a black box. Days 15–35 go inside the index, HNSW, IVF, product quantization, DiskANN, the machinery that makes search over a billion vectors possible. Days 36–55 are quality: reranking, chunking strategy, query transformation. Days 56–70 are measurement. Days 71–85 are production. Days 86–100 are the research frontier and the papers themselves.

Tomorrow we walk the full pipeline stage by stage and name the failure mode at each one, so that for the rest of the course, when something is broken, you have a systematic place to look.
summary: Why a frozen model can't answer questions about your data, why fine-tuning is the wrong fix, and the two clocks (indexing time and query time) that every technique in this course runs on.
title: What RAG actually is: the open-book exam
